subChunks.title: Capstone Project: Build a Production-Grade Distributed System
subChunks.hookHtml: You have completed the SENIOR tier. JVM internals, memory management, concurrency, performance, profiling, distributed systems, messaging, event-driven architecture, resilience patterns, system design, observability, CI/CD, containers, cloud, security engineering, DDD, and technical decision making — all of it converges here. Build something that demonstrates you can engineer at the system level, not just the service level.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Sets This Apart From the JUNIOR Capstone

The JUNIOR capstone demonstrated engineering judgment at the service level: layered architecture, REST design, testing, logging. The SENIOR capstone demonstrates systems thinking: how multiple services communicate, how failures are handled gracefully, how the system is observable, how it scales, and how architectural decisions are made and documented.

Project Options

Option A: Event-Driven Order Platform

A multi-service system: an order service receives orders via REST and publishes OrderPlaced events. An inventory service subscribes and emits InventoryReserved or OutOfStock events. A notification service sends (simulated) emails on relevant events. Requirements: in-memory pub/sub (as built in the messaging lessons), circuit breaker protecting downstream calls, structured logging with correlation IDs (MDC), at least 10 service-layer tests, and an ADR documenting the choreography choice over orchestration.

Option B: Real-Time Leaderboard Service

A tournament leaderboard API that handles high-read, low-write workloads. Players submit scores via REST; the leaderboard serves the top-N players with sub-100ms latency. Requirements: in-memory Redis-like sorted structure, cache-aside pattern with simulated cache and backing store, bulkhead limiting concurrent expensive recomputations, metric counters (rate/errors/duration tracked in memory), and a system design document explaining the scaling strategy for 100K concurrent users.

Option C: Resilient Spell Enrichment Pipeline

A pipeline that enriches raw spell data from multiple upstream sources (simulated as in-memory services). For each spell, it calls a damage calculator, a lore service, and a classification service. Requirements: parallel enrichment using CompletableFuture, circuit breaker on each upstream, retry with exponential backoff, bulkhead per upstream, structured logging with trace ID per enrichment job, DLQ for failed enrichments, and at least 12 service-layer tests.

Option D: Distributed Cache with Consistency Guarantees

Implement a two-node in-memory distributed cache (two Java instances communicating via a simulated network — in-memory message passing). The cache supports get/put/invalidate. Requirements: implement both CP mode (refuse reads during simulated partition) and AP mode (serve stale during partition), document the trade-off with an ADR, demonstrate eventual consistency with a test that shows stale reads resolving after partition heals, and include cache statistics (hit rate, miss rate, eviction count).

Option E: Event-Sourced Audit System

An event-sourced spell audit log. Every mutation to a spell is recorded as an immutable event. The system supports: current state queries (replay events), temporal queries (state at a given timestamp), and projection generation (aggregate stats by element, by tier). Requirements: append-only event log (no delete/update on events), at least 3 different projection types, snapshot mechanism to avoid full replay, bounded context separation between the event store and the query projection layer, and full test coverage of the projection logic.

Mandatory SENIOR Engineering Requirements

  1. Distributed thinking: the system handles failure scenarios — at least one resilience pattern implemented and tested
  2. Observability: structured logging with correlation IDs; at least one metrics counter/timer tracked in memory
  3. Concurrency: meaningful use of CompletableFuture, ExecutorService, or concurrent data structures (not just thread-per-request)
  4. Testing: at least 12 JUnit 5 tests including failure scenarios (circuit open, partition, DLQ routing)
  5. Documentation: one ADR for a significant design decision made during the project
  6. Trade-off reasoning: a written section explaining two architectural decisions and what they optimise for
  7. Security: at least one security concern identified and addressed (auth, input validation, PII in logs)

storyBeats.text: The SENIOR graduation chamber has a different kind of shelf. Not programs, not APIs — but architecture diagrams, ADR folders, and deployment pipelines. The items on this shelf survived incidents: the annotation reads 'circuit breaker prevented cascade failure on 14 March' and 'leaderboard handled 80K concurrent tournament users without degradation.' These are not just things that worked — they are things that worked under pressure.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Rael
storyBeats.text: A JUNIOR project shows you can build a service. A SENIOR project shows you can design a system. The difference is in what you think about before writing a line of code: how does it fail? How does it scale? How will the next engineer understand it when you are gone? How will you know it is healthy? These questions do not show up in the code — they show up in the ADRs, the tests, the observability, and the architecture diagrams.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Rael
storyBeats.text: Every senior project we review, we look at the failure handling first. Not the happy path — the failure path. What happens when the inventory service is down? What happens when the cache is full? What happens when the enrichment takes 30 seconds instead of 200ms? If your answer is 'the whole system stops,' you have not yet thought at the senior level.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Rael
storyBeats.text: The ADR is not bureaucracy. It is clarity. When you write 'we chose choreography over orchestration because our team currently lacks the tooling to visualise orchestrated saga state,' you have made the constraint explicit. When that constraint changes, the ADR tells you why the original choice was made and whether it still applies. That is professional engineering.

Rael steps back and looks at the full SENIOR tier wall — concurrency, distributed systems, resilience, observability, CI/CD, containers, cloud, security, DDD. 'The LEAD tier is different again. It is not about writing better code or designing better systems. It is about enabling other engineers to do both — at scale, across teams, across years. The work becomes invisible. The impact multiplies.'

learningObjectives: Design and implement a multi-component system demonstrating distributed system patterns
Apply at least two resilience patterns (circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, timeout) in a realistic failure scenario
Implement structured observability: correlation IDs in logs and at least one meaningful metric
Write an ADR for a significant design decision and articulate the trade-offs explicitly
commonMistakes: Testing only the happy path — failure scenarios (circuit open, partition, DLQ routing) are where SENIOR engineering shows
Building concurrency as an afterthought rather than designing for it from the start
Writing an ADR after the decision is implemented — the value is in thinking through alternatives before committing
Treating observability as optional — correlation IDs and metrics are required, not suggested
assessmentCriteria: The system handles at least one failure scenario gracefully with a resilience pattern — no cascade failure
All log lines in a request carry a correlation ID (MDC); at least one metric is tracked
Concurrency is used meaningfully: parallel operations, thread-safe data structures, or CompletableFuture composition
At least 12 JUnit 5 tests including failure scenarios; no trivial pass-through tests
One complete ADR with Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, and Options Considered
A trade-off write-up explaining two architectural decisions with explicit optimisation criteria
One security concern identified and addressed (not just mentioned)
subChunks.miniProject:
Extension: Production Readiness Hardening

Once your core project works, add one or more of these:

  • Saga with compensation — implement a distributed transaction using the saga pattern with a compensating action for rollback on failure (e.g. reserve inventory fails → cancel order)
  • Health endpoint — implement GET /health returning system component status (each downstream service: UP/DOWN/DEGRADED) with overall status: HEALTHY/DEGRADED/DOWN
  • Event replay — for event-sourced projects, add a replay endpoint that reconstructs state from a given timestamp, demonstrating temporal queries
  • Chaos testing — write a test that randomly fails upstream calls and verifies the system degrades gracefully (circuit opens, DLQ receives, metrics increment)
  • Performance baseline — use System.nanoTime to establish a baseline throughput (requests per second) under simulated load and document it in a PERFORMANCE.md
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Present your SENIOR capstone as if in a staff engineering review. Walk through: the problem you were solving, the key architectural decisions (with trade-offs stated explicitly), how failures are handled, how the system is observable, and what you would do differently. Be specific — name patterns, name classes, name the decisions in your ADR.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Architecture design exercise — complete before writing any code:

  1. Name your chosen project option (A through E)
  2. Draw or describe the component diagram: list every service/class, what tier (domain/service/infrastructure/presentation) it belongs to, and its primary responsibility
  3. Identify the three most likely failure scenarios in your system and describe which resilience pattern handles each
  4. Describe your correlation ID implementation: how it is generated, where it is stored (MDC), and which layer clears it
  5. Write a draft ADR for the most significant design decision in your project
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Example plan for Option A (Event-Driven Order Platform):

1. Project: Event-Driven Order Platform

2. Component diagram:
   OrderController (Presentation) — REST endpoints; delegates to OrderService
   OrderService (Business Logic) — validates orders, publishes OrderPlaced events; uses circuit breaker for EventBus
   InventoryService (Business Logic) — subscribes to OrderPlaced; emits InventoryReserved or OutOfStock
   NotificationService (Business Logic) — subscribes to InventoryReserved; sends simulated email
   EventBus (Infrastructure) — in-memory pub/sub; routes events by type to subscribers; sends to DLQ on handler failure
   DeadLetterQueue (Infrastructure) — captures failed event deliveries for inspection
   Order (Domain) — id, items, status, correlationId
   InventoryItem (Domain) — productId, stockLevel

3. Three failure scenarios:
   a. EventBus handler throws (e.g. InventoryService unavailable)
      Pattern: Dead Letter Queue — failed events captured, main flow unblocked, can be replayed after fix
   b. OrderService calls EventBus excessively (EventBus overloaded)
      Pattern: Circuit Breaker on EventBus call from OrderService — opens after 5 failures, fail fast for 30s
   c. Multiple concurrent orders for the same item cause oversell
      Pattern: Synchronized block on inventory check-and-decrement, or pessimistic lock equivalent

4. Correlation ID:
   Generated: UUID.randomUUID() at OrderController before any processing
   Stored: MDC.put('correlationId', id) immediately; passed as field in Order domain object
   Propagated: OrderService passes correlationId to event payload; InventoryService reads it from event and puts in own MDC
   Cleared: MDC.clear() in finally block at the Controller layer for the main request thread;
             each async handler clears its own MDC in finally

5. Draft ADR:
   # ADR-0001: Choreography over Orchestration for Order Flow
   ## Status: Accepted
   ## Context: Three services must coordinate on order placement. Need to choose coordination style.
   ## Decision: Choreography — each service listens for events and reacts independently.
   ## Consequences:
   Positive: services fully decoupled, can be developed and deployed independently, easy to add notification types.
   Negative: overall flow invisible in code; debugging requires correlating events across services.
   ## Options Considered:
   Orchestration: central OrderSaga coordinates all services.
   Rejected: adds a stateful orchestrator as a dependency; not justified for 3-service flow with current team tooling.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Build your chosen SENIOR capstone project. When complete, save it to your profile using the 'Save Project' button above. Your submission should include:

  • Full source code (paste or link to GitHub repository)
  • Architecture description (one paragraph per component with its responsibility and the layer it belongs to)
  • Failure handling documentation: list each failure scenario and which pattern handles it
  • One complete ADR (use the standard template from the Technical Decision Making lesson)
  • Test summary: list your 12+ test cases with brief descriptions covering failure scenarios
  • Trade-off write-up: two architectural decisions, what each optimises for, and what is sacrificed
subChunks.modelAnswer:
A strong SENIOR capstone demonstrates:

✅ Multi-component system with clear boundaries — no single-class blob
✅ At least one resilience pattern implemented and tested under failure (circuit breaker opening, DLQ receiving, retry completing)
✅ Correlation IDs in MDC propagated across all log lines in a request chain
✅ Meaningful concurrency — parallel enrichment, thread-safe counters, or CompletableFuture chaining
✅ 12+ JUnit 5 tests including at least 4 failure scenarios
✅ One complete ADR with all sections filled
✅ Explicit trade-off reasoning: 'we chose X which optimises for Y at the cost of Z'
✅ One security concern addressed (not just listed)
✅ No cascade failure — a single component failure does not bring down the whole system

What reviewers look for specifically:
- The failure tests are as thorough as the happy-path tests
- The ADR identifies a genuinely interesting trade-off, not an obvious choice
- Concurrency is correct (no race conditions on shared state)
- The correlation ID appears in all log lines across all component calls in the same request
- The trade-off write-up shows the candidate understands what they sacrificed, not just what they gained

questions.questionHtml: Which SENIOR-tier requirement most distinguishes a SENIOR capstone from a JUNIOR capstone?
options: Failure handling, concurrency, observability, and documented trade-off reasoning at the system level
Using Spring Boot instead of plain Java
questions.correctAnswer: Failure handling, concurrency, observability, and documented trade-off reasoning at the system level
questions.explanationHtml: The JUNIOR capstone demonstrates service-level engineering: layered architecture, REST design, validation, testing, logging. The SENIOR capstone elevates to system-level thinking: how does it fail gracefully? How do multiple components coordinate? How is it observable across components? How were the architectural decisions made and documented? These concerns don't appear in a single service — they emerge from designing across service boundaries.

questions.questionHtml: Your event-driven Order Platform is in production. The InventoryService crashes. What is the expected behaviour of a well-designed system with a Dead Letter Queue?
options: All orders fail immediately with a 500 error
The OrderService stops accepting orders until InventoryService recovers
OrderPlaced events are placed in the DLQ; the OrderService continues accepting orders; events are replayed when InventoryService recovers
The circuit breaker prevents any orders from being placed
questions.correctAnswer: OrderPlaced events are placed in the DLQ; the OrderService continues accepting orders; events are replayed when InventoryService recovers
questions.explanationHtml: With a DLQ, failed event deliveries are captured rather than blocking or losing them. The main flow continues (orders are accepted, events published). When InventoryService recovers, the DLQ contents are replayed and processed. This is the key advantage of async event-driven systems over synchronous REST calls: failures in downstream consumers don't block the upstream producer.

questions.questionHtml: A SENIOR capstone review finds: 12 tests all pass on the happy path, zero tests for failure scenarios. The circuit breaker code exists but has no tests. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: The project meets SENIOR standards — 12 tests is the minimum required
The project is incomplete — untested resilience code may be wrong, and failure scenarios are where SENIOR engineering actually shows
Add one more test and the project will pass
Failure scenario tests are optional at SENIOR level
questions.correctAnswer: The project is incomplete — untested resilience code may be wrong, and failure scenarios are where SENIOR engineering actually shows
questions.explanationHtml: Untested circuit breaker code may be syntactically correct but logically wrong — the state machine transitions could be buggy, the threshold could be off-by-one, or the HALF-OPEN recovery could be broken. The whole value of resilience patterns is that they work when failures actually occur. Testing only happy paths on a system designed for failure handling is a fundamental gap that should be addressed before calling it SENIOR-level work.
